evals.prompt: We run ~40 microservices across 3 product teams on EC2 today and we're moving to EKS. Traffic is spiky, teams want autonomy, and we expect the service count to double in 12 months. Should we run one shared EKS cluster or split per team, and what compute model (Karpenter, MNG, Fargate, Auto Mode) should we default to? Explain the tradeoffs.
expectations: The output recommends a shared multi-tenant EKS cluster as the default over per-team clusters for this scale.
The output calls out per-team namespace isolation explicitly, with at least two of: RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota.
The output recommends Karpenter (or EKS Auto Mode) as the default compute model over pure MNG or Fargate.
The output cites at least one concrete reason for Karpenter (or EKS Auto Mode) as the default compute model, such as consolidation, instance flexibility, or faster scale-up for spiky traffic.

The output recommends running system/platform components (e.g. CoreDNS, Karpenter controller, ingress controller) on a stable managed node group or Fargate rather than on Karpenter-managed workload nodes.

The output names at least one concrete trigger that would justify splitting into multiple clusters (e.g. strict compliance/data-residency boundary, blast-radius isolation for a critical workload, or drastically different upgrade cadences).

The output mentions a path for tenant autonomy that is not cluster-per-team (e.g. namespace-as-a-service, GitOps per-team app-of-apps, or platform abstractions) so teams can move fast on a shared cluster.
Does not recommend kube2iam.

knowledge_assertions.context: Must recommend Karpenter as primary compute engine for spiky workloads: the word must sit next to a recommendation or default phrase, since the prompt itself names Karpenter
Namespace isolation must include network policies
Multi-tenant clusters need resource quotas per namespace
RBAC is foundational for multi-tenant namespace isolation
System components should run on stable managed nodes (or Fargate), not Karpenter-managed: the node group must be tied to system components, since the prompt itself names MNG and Fargate
Must cite Karpenter disruption-specific consolidation mechanics, not just generic benefits: consolidation must be tied to what it does (cost, utilization, fewer or empty nodes), not only named
Must name a concrete trigger for cluster splitting: the trigger must sit next to a separate or dedicated cluster, not only be mentioned

evals.prompt: Review this EKS setup for production readiness. We have a single managed node group of 2 m5.large on-demand nodes in one AZ, no Pod Disruption Budgets defined, no ingress controller installed yet (we're hitting pods via NodePort), and application IAM permissions are attached directly to the node IAM role. What should we fix, in priority order?
expectations: The output identifies the single-AZ / two-node configuration as a high-priority reliability issue.
The output recommends spreading nodes across multiple AZs (at least two) with topology spread constraints or equivalent.
The output recommends adding Pod Disruption Budgets for production workloads with more than one replica.
The output gives at least one concrete example Pod Disruption Budget target (e.g. minAvailable 50% for stateless, maxUnavailable 1 for stateful quorum).
The output flags NodePort as inappropriate for production ingress.
The output recommends the AWS Load Balancer Controller with ALB or NLB (or Gateway API) as the replacement for NodePort.
The output flags attaching application IAM permissions to the node role as a security anti-pattern.
The output recommends migrating to EKS Pod Identity (preferred) or IRSA per workload.
The output presents the fixes in a prioritized order (e.g. reliability first, then security, then ingress) rather than as an unordered list.
Does not recommend kube2iam.

knowledge_assertions.context: Must recommend Pod Identity as the preferred approach for workloads on Linux EC2 nodes (IRSA stays supported and is needed on Fargate and Windows)
Must mention IRSA as alternative/predecessor to Pod Identity
Multi-AZ spread should use topology spread constraints
Must recommend PDBs for production workloads: the term must sit next to an add or define phrase, since the prompt itself says 'no Pod Disruption Budgets defined'
PDB recommendation must include a concrete spec example
Must recommend AWS LBC over NodePort for production ingress

knowledge_assertions.pattern: NodePort[^.\n]{0,80}(not (suitable|recommended|appropriate|meant|intended|for production)|inappropriate|anti.?pattern|avoid|replace|insecure|risk|bypass|unsuitable|exposes)|(avoid|replace|move (off|away from)|migrate (off|away from)|stop using|instead of|rather than)[^.\n]{0,40}NodePort
knowledge_assertions.context: Must explicitly flag NodePort as the anti-pattern being replaced: the word must sit next to a flag or replace phrase, since the prompt itself names NodePort
Should mention NodePort high port range (30000-32767) as a concrete detail
Must frame node-role IAM as a security risk, not just a recommendation

evals.prompt: We run an e-commerce platform on EKS. Next month we have a big flash sale: at a fixed time our push notification fires and traffic steps almost instantly to many multiples of baseline, with a few secondary peaks over the following hours. Last time, a load test that hit our target request rate still didn't prevent an outage. How do we get the cluster ready to absorb this kind of surge, and how should we think about pre-scaling and load testing?
expectations: The output recommends scheduled/proactive pre-scaling ahead of the known event time (raising replica floors or desired counts before the trigger) rather than relying solely on reactive metric-driven autoscaling to catch up.
The output distinguishes the spike SHAPE (near-instant step / rate of arrival) from magnitude.
The output warns against scaling down or consolidating in the trough between peaks.
The output addresses capacity assurance ahead of the event, at least one of: service-quota pre-checks, On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCR), or load-balancer warm-up.

The output explains the load-test-realism lesson: a test passing on request rate can still miss a resource-consumption (e.g. memory) failure from a new/changed access pattern, so scenarios must cover consumption shapes.
The output says load-test findings must be acted on before the event.
The output stays advisory: it does NOT invent a specific maximum absorbable step, headroom number, or sizing verdict for the cluster.
The output gives no GREEN, AMBER or RED rating per area: it is a planning aid, not a scored audit.

knowledge_assertions.context: Must recommend scheduled/proactive pre-scaling ahead of the known event time (not just reactive autoscaling): the prompt's own 'pre-scaling' and a bare scheduler mention do not pass
Must frame the surge as a rate/step-shape problem (and/or the multi-peak trough), not just peak magnitude
Must address capacity assurance ahead of the event (quotas, ODCR, or LB warm-up)
Must explain load-test realism as consumption-shape (e.g. memory) scenario coverage, not just request rate: memory must sit next to the load test or scenario, not only be mentioned

Surge readiness is advisory/descriptive: it must NOT emit an eks-operation-review-style scored audit. This regex catches a per-area colour VERDICT as a table cell (trailing pipe optional, so a borderless GFM row ('| Autoscaling | AMBER') still matches), an area label followed by a single colour ('Networking: RED'), plus a 'score each area' / 'maturity report' instruction: the structural signature of a scored audit. A guard spares a prose disclaimer that merely names the scheme, including the 'not an operation review: GREEN/AMBER/RED are out of scope' shape: the `(?!\s*[/|])` lookahead on the label-then-colour branch skips slash-joined colour lists, where the colour is part of a scheme name rather than standing alone as a verdict. A leading colour-then-colon verdict ('AMBER: ...') is an accepted documented miss: a branch for that shape false-fired on legitimate blue/green deployment prose ('Green: the new stack that takes traffic...'), so the judge expectation 'The output gives no GREEN, AMBER or RED rating per area' backstops it. Regex flags: case-insensitive, except the colour words, which are case-sensitive (the eks-operation-review vocabulary is uppercase).

evals.prompt: We run several EKS clusters (managed node groups and one EKS Auto Mode cluster) and we keep hearing about security fixes late. How should our platform team set up security operations: which sources to watch, how often to patch add-ons, node images and container images, how to handle an urgent security fix, and what our build pipeline should do so one bad dependency cannot spread far?
expectations: The output names concrete sources to watch across layers (for example AWS security bulletins, the Kubernetes CVE feed, node OS advisories, add-on releases, image scan findings).
The output recommends routing the watched sources into alerting rather than periodic review.
The output separates a normal patch cadence from an emergency path for security fixes.
The output says the emergency path for security fixes still tests in non-production before production.
The output explains that on EKS Auto Mode AWS patches the node image but existing nodes keep the old build until they are replaced (drift to the new AMI, node expiry, or planned rotation).
The output recommends digest-pinned base images moved through review.
The output recommends installing dependencies from a committed lockfile in an isolated build step.
The output recommends rebuilding on a cadence.
The output gives the reason for rebuilding on a cadence: package scanners (such as ECR enhanced scanning) match only packages tracked in CVE advisories.
The output routes live checks (whether a cluster is exposed to a specific advisory, live event response) to eks-security rather than claiming to inspect the clusters itself.

knowledge_assertions.context: Must name AWS security bulletins as a source to watch
Must describe a separate path for urgent security fixes
Must recommend pinning images by digest
Must recommend building from a committed lockfile
Must route live exposure checks to eks-security
